task_brief: Technique work on three-dimensional construction. Technique: test a material or mark-making process through three-dimensional construction, then use observable evidence to explain or revise a learner-owned decision. Complete the bounded study yourself before asking for a cue.
primary_task: Target for this apply session: Apply three-dimensional construction independently in a new representation, text, situation, or design constraint. Use subject-appropriate evidence or representation to communicate understanding of three-dimensional construction. Check, revise, or improve work about three-dimensional construction using stated success criteria. Closing evidence check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about three-dimensional construction; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. What three-dimensional construction means here: A studio technique is a repeatable material action used on purpose, not a required personal style. 1. Independent creation: Create a fresh, bounded work involving three-dimensional construction. State an intent, choose at least two relevant relationships, preserve one intermediate state, check the result, and make or deliberately decline one revision with a reason. 2. Critique: Describe before judging. Locate evidence, compare it with the maker’s stated intent, ask one genuine question, and offer options; the maker keeps final authority. A private self-critique receives full credit. 3. Reflection: Compare an earlier and later state. Name the choice that changed, cite what became visible, audible, notated, or workable, and state the next revision or reason to keep the result. Your choices remain yours: Different subject, safe material route, mark or construction vocabulary, degree of finish, revision that serves the stated intent choices are valid when the learner meets objective constraints and supports the result with evidence. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about three-dimensional construction. It is part of "Techniques, Media, and Craftsmanship". Later days in this unit cover other things, like drawing techniques. Before you stop, do this check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about three-dimensional construction; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. In grade 4, try the steps yourself before you ask for help. Give a reason in your own words for at least one choice. A labelled drawing or a spoken answer counts fully.

presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. Keeping the work entirely to yourself, showing it to one parent or trusted adult, or submitting it as a file with no one watching are all full-credit options. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or voice recording is required at any point in this task, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available for spoken reflection, explanation, or critique and scores the same. Use a labelled visual, tactile, constructed, or accessible digital work to preserve the making target; prose alone does not claim visual or material technique evidence. You may describe the work in writing and have one trusted adult verify a physical artifact without photographing you or your home. No microphone, camera, or recording is required.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any material you did not create yourself must be in the public domain, openly licensed, or used as a short cited excerpt for study — reproduce no more than the point requires, credit the maker and the source, and never copy full lyrics, a complete score, or a whole image and present it as your own.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: This work takes more than one sitting. Ask for a simple checklist with dates so you know what to do next. Keeping track is not part of your grade.
You can take a break, stretch, or come back to this later. That does not lower your score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Protect hearing, ventilation, tool safety, copyright, cultural context, and respectful representation.
No public performance, voice recording, photo, or camera use is ever required; provide a private, written, or no-audio alternative for every task.
Use only original student work, public-domain material, or properly licensed excerpts; never reproduce full copyrighted lyrics, sheet music, or protected works.
The final product must remain the student’s own authorship; adult or AI assistance may support planning and feedback but must not create the graded work.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting three-dimensional construction.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile/concrete model, or teacher demonstration.

remediation: Route 1: Reduce three-dimensional construction to three locatable events, areas, steps, or decisions. Label the intended effect beside each and underline the one tool pressure relationship that should carry it. Use a separate small study, four-event loop, thumbnail, evidence table, or paper plan. The adult may model the noticing process on different material but may not change the learner’s work. Check yourself: Point to or name the exact tool pressure evidence before deciding whether it serves the intent. New attempt: Put the support away and make a new arrangement, passage, response, or plan; record what the new evidence shows. Route 2: Return to the last understandable state. Hold every relationship steady except one chosen feature from tool pressure, direction, layering, joining, edge, surface, proportion, and safe control; predict what that single change should do. Test the feature on scrap paper, a silent count, a two-event rehearsal loop, movable shapes, or a short evidence sentence before changing the scored work. Check yourself: Name what stayed the same, what changed, and the first observable result—without using “better” as the evidence. New attempt: Create a different small case using the same one-variable method, then transfer the finding to the original task only if it serves the learner’s intent.
extension: Apply three-dimensional construction under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on three-dimensional construction rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays private by default and uses only original, public-domain, or properly cited material. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.

concept_instruction.title: What three-dimensional construction means here
concept_instruction.body: A studio technique is a repeatable material action used on purpose, not a required personal style.

concept_instruction.title: How the relationship changes the result
concept_instruction.body: Pressure, angle, speed, sequence, moisture, layering, or joining changes the visible and tactile result; isolating one variable makes cause and effect easier to notice.

concept_instruction.title: Choice and tradeoff
concept_instruction.body: More control can increase clarity, while a looser action may preserve energy or texture. The useful choice depends on intent and safe material limits. Worked example: Three short studies that change only pressure reveal which marks stay light, become dark, or damage the surface. Non-example: Copying a polished image without recording setup, actions, and changes hides the technique the lesson is meant to teach.

technique_sequence.why: Pressure, angle, speed, sequence, moisture, layering, or joining changes the visible and tactile result; isolating one variable makes cause and effect easier to notice.

technique_sequence.action: Complete one small controlled study or rehearsal loop.
technique_sequence.notice: Keep most relationships stable so one decision remains readable.
technique_sequence.why: A bounded test makes cause and effect easier to notice.

technique_sequence.action: Transfer the idea to a fresh work, excerpt, source detail, or project decision.

technique_sequence.why: Evidence protects creative variation and learner authority.

common_technique_errors.observable_mismatch: The stated intent for three-dimensional construction is present, but the record does not yet locate tool pressure, direction, layering, joining, edge, surface, proportion, and safe control that supports it.
common_technique_errors.not_an_error_when: The learner supports a different, ambiguous, subtle, or intentionally open effect with observable evidence.

common_technique_errors.observable_mismatch: Several relationships changed at once, so the learner cannot yet tell which choice caused the observed effect.
common_technique_errors.not_an_error_when: The task is an intentionally exploratory diagnostic and no causal claim is being scored.
